name: Silverfir-nano
baseline: wasmtime Cranelift 47.0.2; V8 TurboFan (Node.js 25.9); wasm3; wasmi 2.0.0-beta.7
workload: 15 WASI benchmark metrics (CoreMark, SHA-256, bzip2, LZ4, sqlite speedtest1, Lua scripts, mandelbrot, c-ray, STREAM) self-timed for 2 s on an Apple M4; JIT compared with optimizing compilers and interpreter compared with interpreters.
claimed_speedup: JIT at parity with Cranelift and V8: best-of-four over 15 metrics is Cranelift 9, Silverfir 4, V8 2; leads on SHA-256 250.6 vs Cranelift 216.8 MB/s (+16%) and bzip2 30.68 vs 26.86 MB/s (+14%); CoreMark 44,958 vs Cranelift 45,874 vs V8 44,378; beats V8 on mandelbrot 1.68x. Interpreter: CoreMark 8,586.4 vs wasm3 4,268 and wasmi 5,482; wins 14 of 15 metrics by 1.16-2.01x over wasm3 and 1.07-2.41x over wasmi (margin over the faster rival 1.07-1.69x, median about 1.39x).
compiler_and_flags: Guests: wasi-sdk clang (version not stated) -O2 --target=wasm32-wasip1 via benchmarks/wasi/Makefile, binaries committed and shared by all engines. Silverfir: cargo --release, workspace profile lto=true, codegen-units=1, opt-level=3. wasmtime Cranelift and Winch 47.0.2 built from source with rustc 1.97.0; Node 25.9.0 (V8 14.1.146); wasm3 '~/Dev/wasm3 build-release' (commit and flags not stated); wasmi_cli 2.0.0-beta.7 via cargo install (CoreMark cell 2.0.0-beta.10). Harness: benchmarks/wasi/run_tests.py and run_v8.mjs.
hardware: Apple M4 (macOS)
tradeoffs: no_std runtime with both a JIT and an interpreter on six ISAs (x86_64, ARM64, RISC-V, Thumb-2); flash 337 KiB interpreter and 1,042 KiB JIT on RP2350; Wasm 3.0 features but the interpreter excludes SIMD and GC; Rust, so C++ embedding needs bindings.
caveats: First-party suite, one machine (M4), interpreters are single runs (author says treat as +/-5%) while compiled engines are the mean of two rounds; Cranelift still wins 9 of 15 metrics and is ahead on sqlite and LZ4 decompress (3,478 vs 3,241), so the JIT claim is parity, not a win. Wasmtime 47.0.2 and V8 14.1 are older than current releases (wasmtime v49 was current in September 2026); the numbers are dated 2026-07-24/25 and share no baseline with earlier revisions of the file. CoreMark runs in a non-standard bounded regression mode, except the interpreter CoreMark row, which was refreshed on 2026-08-31 with standalone scores and uses wasmi 2.0.0-beta.10 rather than beta.7. name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (iwasm); Wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (xmrsplayer audio, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max (A12) E-cores.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), M4 Max E-cores: wasm3 1.01, WAMR fast-interp 1.63, Wasmtime Pulley 2.09, WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; A12 E-cores: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68, WasmEdge 9.28. About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4 (derived from page data). Page text: 'wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0), no WASI sources; WAMR cmake Release -O3 FAST_INTERP only (AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off); Pulley rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with no JIT or AOT tier: far slower than compiling runtimes. In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is wasm3 16.51x vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x. Very cheap startup: same suite startup geomean wasm3 lazy 2.77x vs WAMR fast-interp 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the benchmark tested it supports only tail calls and extended-const. Maintainer states the project is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Result is interpreter versus interpreter: wasm3 is not faster than JIT/AOT Wasmtime, Wasmer or V8 (its own docs/Performance.md CoreMark table, 2019-2020 on an i5-8250U and labelled historical by the project, has wasmtime 0.8.0 and Wasmer Cranelift 4.0x faster and wasm-micro-runtime 8.1x slower; in the wasmi-benchmarks suite on an AMD EPYC 7763 its execute geomean is 16.51 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15 and V8 1.05, and behind Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02 and Wasmi v2 12.40). The 17-case geomean covers only MVP/scalar code: wasm3 cannot run the SIMD-canonical builds, exceptions, GC, typed references, memory64 or multi-memory, and WAMR leads on the SIMD rows. Instantiation is its weak spot: extended-const modules cost it 116-122x Pulley's time on the M4 (62-85x on the A12). The benchmark author built WAMR with 29 carried patches, WasmEdge with 26 and Pulley from a fork branch with 9 extra commits, while wasm3 v0.9.0 ran unpatched. Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test', native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR. The README still declares a minimal maintenance phase, though September 2026 commits add atomics and an exception-handling API.

name: zwasm
baseline: wasmtime 43.0.1; wasmer 5.0.4; wazero 1.11.0; WasmEdge 0.16.1 (interpreter)
workload: End-to-end wall time of '<runtime> run <module>' (spawn, instantiate, execute WASI _start) with hyperfine on short TinyGo and ClojureWasm guests, plus peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
claimed_speedup: Startup-bound short workloads (mean ms): tinygo/fib zwasm-aot 2.0, interp 2.3, jit 2.8 vs wasmtime 7.2, wazero 7.1, wasmer 12.0, WasmEdge 16.5. Peak RSS on tinygo/fib: zwasm-aot 2.1 MB, jit 3.2, interp 2.7 vs wazero 8.7, wasmtime 13.3, WasmEdge 23.7, wasmer 27.5 ('4-12x less').
compiler_and_flags: zwasm built with Zig 0.16.0 (pinned in flake.nix) via zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; comparators wasmtime 43.0.1, wazero 1.11.0, wasmer 5.0.4, WasmEdge 0.16.1 pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench; hyperfine 5 runs plus 3 warmup; peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (Mac aarch64), one host
tradeoffs: Single-pass JIT, interpreter and AOT backends with Wasm 3.0 and WASI 0.2/0.3; small footprint and fast startup traded for peak throughput.
caveats: The win is cold-start latency and memory footprint only. The same doc shows the optimizing JITs ahead on sustained compute: wasmtime/wasmer/wazero beat zwasm-jit/aot by about 1.5-3.9x (shootout/fib2 zwasm-jit 1077 ms vs wasmtime 700 ms; matrix 343 vs 88 ms; base64 781 vs 57 ms, about 13.7x). The startup rows time a whole process (spawn + instantiate + run) on sub-10 ms guests, so they measure startup, not execution; the zwasm-aot row excludes its one-off compile step while comparator rows include their JIT compile, and the doc does not say whether wasmtime/wasmer compilation caches were on. Single host (Apple M4 Pro, macOS); wasmer only on aarch64-darwin. The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, zwasm v2.7.0 with the JIT compiled out) puts zwasm's interpreter at a geomean 8.47x the fastest runtime's CPU time on M4 Max E-cores (wasm3 1.01, WAMR 1.63, WasmEdge 8.42). Embeddable from C/C++ via the standard wasm-c-api.

name: WAVM
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer (LLVM, Cranelift, Singlepass backends) and V8 (Node.js)
workload: libsodium 1.0.18 built to WASI (clang 11.1.0, wasm-opt -O4) and run on every runtime with ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; per-test timings across the crypto and codec test suite.
claimed_speedup: Page text (macOS x86_64): 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test' and 'about 15% faster than wasmer' (LLVM backend); V8 (Node.js) second; Lucet slowest. Total-time chart (summed from the per-test logs in 2021-Q1/output/macos-x86_64, derived from page data): wavm 4.63, node 5.23 (1.13x wavm), wasmer-llvm 5.44 (1.17x), wasmtime 6.65 (1.43x), wasmer-cranelift 10.70, wasmer-jit 10.98, wasmer-singlepass 11.11, lucet 11.61 (2.5x), native 2.04 (sums of the logged per-test times in units of 1e12; the chart plots the same totals rescaled). Per-test geomean of time vs wavm (derived from page data, 58 tests): wasmtime 1.47x, node 1.20x, wasmer-llvm 1.09x, lucet 2.47x, wasmer-singlepass 2.56x. Linux x86_64 LLVM-runtime run: 'wavm remains undethroned, but SSVM comes really close'.
compiler_and_flags: All runtimes compiled from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js from stock binaries); libsodium 1.0.18-stable built with LLVM 11.1.0 (Homebrew) via ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench, output pre-optimized with wasm-opt -O4; native and WebAssembly builds use the same default optimization flags; runtimes invoked through libsodium's test/default/wasi-test-wrapper.sh.
hardware: macOS x86_64 laptop (CPU model not stated) and a Linux x86_64 machine for the LLVM-runtime comparison
tradeoffs: LLVM-based compilation: the EOS VM README (github.com/AntelopeIO/eos-vm) calls WAVM compilation times 'extremely long and unpredictable'; LLVM dependency.
caveats: Data are from February 2021 on an unnamed Intel macOS laptop plus an unnamed Linux x86_64 machine; WAVM was not run on ARM. name: LFI (Lightweight Fault Isolation)

compiler_and_flags: LLVM/Clang 15.0.7 with the LFI rewriter for native, LFI and Wasm builds; Wasm bytecode further optimized with wasm-opt, SIMD128 enabled, bounds checks replaced by guard pages; Wasmtime run in AOT mode. Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Apple M1): Julia 1.10.0 nqueen 3.02 s, matmul 0.76 s, sudoku 2.18 s, bedcov 1.96 s vs luajit 5.31/2.66/4.48/10.52 s, PyPy 7.3.14 6.91/4.89/8.82/6.27 s, Java 20.0.1 3.92/1.14/3.20/3.04 s, Node 21.5.0 3.73/2.88/3.77/2.45 s (faster than all four on all four tasks).

hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G; plb2: Apple M1 MacBook Pro
tradeoffs: Per-process JIT warmup and large footprint (kostya bench.b base RSS about 244 MB vs 2.5 MB for LuaJIT); package precompilation latency; garbage collected; embedding in C++ goes through the libjulia C API and is heavier than embedding LuaJIT.
caveats: Workload specific: Java beats Julia on kostya's bench.b and mandel.b, and in kostya's other tests Julia loses to most baselines: base64 3.085 s vs Node.js 0.635 s and Java 1.435 s (Julia does beat PyPy 3.534 s there); primes 0.680 s vs Java 0.161 s, Node.js 0.207 s, luajit 0.309 s and PyPy 0.617 s; JSON (JSON3) 0.700 s vs Node.js 0.374 s, Java DSL-JSON 0.571 s and PyPy 0.606 s. In plb2 Julia beats all four baselines. The kostya run uses --check-bounds=no (bounds checks removed) and plb2's Julia sources use @inbounds in hot loops, which other languages' sources do not. The kostya 'no BLAS' matmul source is not a plain triple loop: it uses @simd ivdep and @fastmath (allowing reassociation and vectorized FMA, which Java and V8 cannot do) and wraps the outer loop in Threads.@threads (single-threaded here, since JULIA_RUN passes no -t and sets no JULIA_NUM_THREADS). Julia matmul rows at 0.12-0.17 s use BLAS and are not comparable. The kostya brainfuck bf.jl scans raw characters and brackets at run time, while the Node, Java and C# versions parse an op tree first, so the code shapes differ. Each program runs a small verify() before the timer starts, which warms the JIT on the same functions, so most compile time is outside the timed region; plb2 includes startup and compile time. kostya's docker/Dockerfile now pins julia-1.12.6 while the README environment lists v1.11.6, so the published numbers predate the current image.

tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler and runtime aimed at embedded systems (x86_64, aarch64, tricore; aarch32 not implemented), written in C++14 with no external dependencies in production code; 187 kB stripped binary (AArch64, Clang 17, macOS). caveats: Result is a normalized unitless quadrant chart; run_bench.py prints wall-clock means and a score of 10000/geomean, but how the 0-1 chart values were derived is not documented, and native clang's compile score is a placeholder 0.5 ('comp. speed N/A'). Harness flaws: the compilation benchmark times the whole process with /usr/bin/time -p (10 ms resolution), so d8 and SpiderMonkey js-shell startup and JS harness load are charged to their compile time while WARP runs as a small native binary, which favours WARP; default is a single run per module (-n 1); the 'V8 Liftoff' runs do not pass --no-wasm-tier-up, so hot code may tier up to TurboFan. name: TruffleRuby
baseline: CRuby 4.0.6 (MRI interpreter), also CRuby with --jit (YJIT)
workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck bench.b, matmul, primes, JSON, base64, run as the same Ruby scripts under each Ruby implementation.
claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet (https://github.com/smarr/are-we-fast-yet/blob/master/docs/performance.md, 2016-06-20, peak performance, runtime factor over Java 1.8.0_91) 'JRuby+Truffle' (the former name of TruffleRuby): geomean 2.36 (sd 0.94, median 2.64, max 4.31) vs Node.js 2.89 (sd 3.33, median 2.54, max 12.25), about 1.22x lower geomean (derived from page data). It is faster than Node.js on only 6 of 14 benchmarks (Bounce 1.41 vs 12.25, DeltaBlue, Havlak 4.31 vs 10.24, NBody, Richards, Sieve 1.62 vs 3.61), and without the Bounce outlier the geomeans are 2.46 vs 2.58, about 1.05x (derived from page data); Node.js has the better median. Its clear AWFY win is over other Rubies: JRuby 12.83 and MRI 45.62. kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks, update 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G): on bench.b, truffleruby 34.0.1 native 5.169 s and JVM 4.645 s beat Lua/luajit 5.686 s and Python/pypy 9.398 s (Node.js 2.954 s is faster). On the other shared tests it is slower: mandel.b 48.381 s vs luajit 31.804 s and pypy 41.153 s; Json 10.618 s vs pypy 0.606 s; Matmul 17.667 s vs pypy 3.263 s; Primes 0.871 s vs luajit 0.309 s and pypy 0.617 s. On Base64 the JVM mode ties PyPy (3.505 s vs 3.534 s). kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X): truffleruby 22.3.1 in JVM mode beats PyPy3 7.3.11 on 6 of 13 benchmarks and LuaJIT 2.1.0-beta3 on 5 of 11, for example binarytrees 0.69 s vs 3.84 s (PyPy) and 6.73 s (LuaJIT), and nbody 0.85 s vs 4.44 s and 1.44 s.
compiler_and_flags: TruffleRuby 34.0.1 native and JVM release tarballs vs CRuby 4.0.6 built with CC=clang ./configure --enable-yjit (docker/Dockerfile); scripts run via `truffleruby`, `ruby`, `ruby --jit`.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid) per README Environment section; base image and interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile
tradeoffs: Needs warm-up and much more memory (bench.b: 197.19 + 693.00 MiB vs 12.12 + 0.00 MiB for CRuby in the kostya tables). README offers two configurations: Native (faster startup) and JVM (better peak performance).
caveats: Mixed against every listed baseline. On AWFY the geomean edge over Node.js comes mostly from Node's Bounce outlier, and Node.js has the better median. On kostya/benchmarks TruffleRuby is slower than LuaJIT and PyPy on 4 of the 6 shared tests (mandel.b, Json, Matmul, Primes), with Matmul 5.4x and Json 17x slower than PyPy. Node.js beats it on every kostya test shown. On kostya/jit-benchmarks 2023 it wins about half the time. AWFY numbers date from 2016, and the paper is co-authored by Benoit Daloze, a TruffleRuby developer, so it is peer-reviewed but not independent. JVM mode has high memory use (about 350 MB base RSS on kostya). plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) lists Ruby only on the proprietary 'Graal EE 23.1.1' build. name: CPython tail-calling interpreter
baseline: CPython computed-goto interpreter loop (same source, default dispatch)
workload: pyperformance suite, CPython built with clang-19, ThinLTO and PGO on AMD64 Ubuntu 22.04; per-benchmark results in gist https://gist.github.com/Fidget-Spinner/497c664eef389622d146d632990b0d21 (main 2228e92da31c vs tail-call 465467f47553, 2025-01-05).
claimed_speedup: After correction: geomean 3-5% faster on pyperformance (issue correction notice; Python 3.14 What's New says 3-5% depending on platform and architecture, baseline Python 3.14 built with Clang 19 without the new interpreter). The original claim of 10% geomean, up to 40% on Python-heavy benchmarks (gist: 1.10x geomean, best 1.46x on scimark_sor, unpickle_list 1.02x slower) was artificially boosted by an LLVM 19 bug that slowed the computed-goto baseline.
compiler_and_flags: clang-19 (needs Clang 19+ on x86-64 and AArch64), ThinLTO and PGO; PGO is said to be especially crucial for the speedup.
hardware: AMD64 machine, Ubuntu 22.04 (CPU model not on the page)
tradeoffs: Needs Clang 19 or newer (x86-64 and AArch64) and PGO to pay off per the issue.
caveats: Baseline is CPython itself, so this is a delta against the incumbent's previous dispatch, not against another implementation. The headline 10%/40% numbers were withdrawn by the authors after an LLVM 19 bug was found; the corrected 3-5% geomean is the figure to use, and even that baseline is the Clang 19 computed-goto build, which issue #158283 measures as 7.7% slower than a GCC 13 build on Linux x86-64 and 11.4% slower with Xcode 16.4 on macOS arm64 (merged dispatch jumps). An independent measurement by Nelson Elhage (blog.nelhage.com, snippet only, blocked here) found only 1.03x on a Raptor Lake i5-13500 and 1.00x on an Apple M1 against a clang-18 computed-goto build. Needs Clang 19+ on x86-64/AArch64 and PGO; opt-in via --with-tail-call-interp. Separately, Python 3.15 What's New reports 15-20% pyperformance geomean on Windows x86-64 with MSVC 18 (Visual Studio 18.1.1) versus the switch-case interpreter on an AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (chart in faster-cpython/ideas results/5800X-msvc.pgo2-vs-msvc.pgo.tc.svg), and the official Windows 64-bit binaries now use the tail-calling interpreter. CPU model absent for the clang claim, so the tier is C.

name: LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
baseline: Node.js 20 (V8) on AWS Lambda
workload: AWS Lambda DynamoDB Put function (example/functions/src/v3-lib.mjs), ARM, 128MB: 64 cold starts and 20000 warm starts, percentiles p0-p100 of Lambda-reported Init Duration plus Function Duration and of HTTP round-trip time; results only as two PNG screenshots in the README.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'up to over 10x faster startup and up to 2x overall lower cost compared to other JavaScript runtimes running on AWS Lambda'. Screenshots (benchmarks/llrt-ddb-put.png vs benchmarks/node20-ddb-put.png, DynamoDB Put, ARM, 128MB, 64 cold starts, 20000 warm starts): cold-start p50 Lambda-reported Init+Function duration 64.16 ms vs 1511.93 ms for Node.js 20 (about 23.6x, derived from page data); cold-start p50 HTTP round trip 235.61 ms vs 1719.00 ms (about 7.3x, derived from page data); warm p50 14.94 vs 33.20 ms (lambda) and 43.72 vs 62.08 ms (HTTP). The 2x cost claim has no numbers on the page.
hardware: AWS Lambda ARM, 128MB memory (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: No JIT, so peak compute is far slower than V8 and not recommended for compute-heavy work; partial Node.js API compatibility; ES2023 only; README marks it experimental and for evaluation purposes.
caveats: Only first-party numbers, shown as screenshots committed once on 2024-01-31 ('Add perf screenshots') and never refreshed, so they reflect the launch-era LLRT against Node.js 20, not current versions of either. The win is cold start, where a no-JIT QuickJS runtime with a bundled SDK wins by design; warm p50 HTTP latency is only about 1.4x better (derived from page data) and CPU-heavy code would favor V8's JIT. The load-test harness that produced the tables is not in the repo (benchmarks/ holds the PNGs, fetch-streaming.mjs and a v8-v7 suite). The README calls LLRT experimental and 'intended only for evaluation purposes', and says it is not a drop-in Node.js replacement (many node: modules missing, e.g. http, tls, worker_threads). Written in Rust on QuickJS, so it is a runtime to adopt, not a C++ library. The '2x lower cost' claim has no published numbers.

compiler_and_flags: nuitka --lto=yes --pgo-c (and --static-libpython=yes for the Python 3 variant); C compiler version for the table not stated (README says GCC 5.1+, Clang or MSVC 2022+ supported).
tradeoffs: Compiles Python to C and still depends on a Python runtime; speedups are modest on dynamic code; needs a C compiler; AGPL-3.0 licence (check implications for compiled output).
caveats: The published table is pystone on Python 2.7 only; the README says Python 3 measurements will follow later, and the pystone3 commands it shows have no published results. pystone is a synthetic benchmark. No CPU model and no C compiler version for the table (a separate README section says clang6 beat gcc-6.3 slightly on Linux and MinGW64 beat MSVC by about 20% on Windows). The documented commands contain a typo for the compiled Python 2 run ('sort -n | head -rn 1', head has no -r option) and the text says 1000 runs while that loop runs 100, so the table cannot have come from the commands exactly as printed. An independent timing in the Shed Skin README shows Nuitka 0.6.16 at 11.4 s on the sieve example (n=100000000), identical to CPython 3.11.0 (11.4 s) and only slightly faster than CPython 3.10.6 (13.4 s), so gains on other workloads can be near zero. Licence is AGPL-3.0 with a runtime exception (LICENSE-RUNTIME.txt) covering the compiled output.

name: Pyston

claimed_speedup: Pyston 'full' (CPython 3.8.12 fork with DynASM JIT): 'roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks'; Pyston 'lite' (JIT extension module): 'roughly 10% faster on macrobenchmarks'.
license: Python-2.0 (CPython license stack: PSF License Version 2 with BeOpen, CNRI and CWI agreements; root LICENSE is CPython's)
tradeoffs: Pyston-full is a CPython 3.8.12 fork with a very-low-overhead JIT (DynASM), quickening, attribute caching and build-process improvements (PGO/BOLT); API compatible but not ABI compatible, so C extensions need recompiling; pyston-lite is a pip-installable JIT extension for CPython 3.7 to 3.10 that stays binary compatible.
caveats: First-party README numbers ('roughly 30%' full, 'roughly 10%' lite) with no CPU, flags, CPython version or run counts; benchmark suite is public (pyston/python-macrobenchmarks, pyperformance manifest 'pyston_standard') but no result table is published in the repo. Baseline is CPython of the 3.7-3.10 era; newer CPython releases are not compared, and PyPy is not compared. Repository description says '(No longer maintained)'; the last code change was the Feb 28, 2023 merge of PR #301 and the Aug 12, 2024 commits only touch issue templates. Licence: the only LICENSE file is CPython's (PSF License Version 2 stack); no Apache-2.0 text was found (no pyston/ or pyston_lite LICENSE, JIT sources such as Python/aot_ceval_jit.c carry no header, PyPI pyston-lite lists no licence); the Apache-2.0 claim likely comes from the separate Pyston v1 repo. Pyston-full is API- but not ABI-compatible with CPython, so C extensions must be recompiled.
